extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy / intellectual history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria used in the comparative evaluation of moral theories (intuitionism vs utilitarianism) and moral practices across historical societies. Focuses on standards for judging virtues, motives, and the origin and application of moral rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctity of continence / chastity as moral ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: A widespread moral sentiment that perfect continence or chastity is sacred and a mark of sanctity; this ideal recurs across diverse ages and creeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text supplies numerous historical examples (Nazarenes and Essenes, Egyptian and Indian priests, Chinese legend of the virgin-mother, Athene and Artemis in Greece, Vestal virgins in Rome, monastic orders). Also notes consequences: Catholic monasticism drew thousands from active life, produced suffering and sometimes crime, and opposed domestic affections—yet reflected a genuine feeling that the purely animal side of our being is lower.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between bodily (sensual) and spiritual (rational) parts of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral systems may rest on a sharp valuation that the spiritual or rational part of human nature is higher than the bodily or sensual part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's moral system and the Pythagorean school treat chastity and suppression of sensuality as virtues; artistic and religious ideals often separate an 'unsullied' spiritual love from earthly sensuality. This distinction underlies many prescriptions (e.g., celibacy in orders) and judgments of moral worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy of moral motives over intellectual or physical interests
rubrics_metrics.description: The view that moral motives should have primacy in a well-ordered life, and that we are under an obligation to develop our moral nature to perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raises the central ethical problem of casuistry—whether any material or intellectual advantage can justify sacrificing the moral nature. The text interrogates extreme versions (which forbid any sacrifice) and argues society generally accepts some trade-offs in favour of civilisation and material progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of some absolute or immutable moral distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are certain acts (e.g., truth vs falsehood) that are so manifestly contrary to moral feelings that they are regarded as wrong even at early stages of moral development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between virtues of degree and moral distinctions that assume sharp definition; acknowledges variation in scrupulosity about these distinctions across periods but maintains a class of acts regarded as intrinsically wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Societal standard as external rule for designating right and wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: Aside from positive commands, the external standard by which acts are designated right or wrong is the level of moral development attained by society—the cultivated higher part of human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one meets the prevailing social standard, one has 'done his duty' externally; surpassing it enters the realm of optional 'counsels of perfection.' This provides a social/legalistic criterion for judging conduct across eras.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of absolute sin (theological casuistry): no end justifies sin
rubrics_metrics.description: A theological doctrine that any undoubted sin is so dreadful in essence and consequence that no material or intellectual advantage can justify it; thus the end never justifies the means when sin is involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to extreme prescriptions (suppression of desires, abstention from social life) and is critiqued as impracticable because, if applied, it would render civilisation impossible (e.g., forbidding wars that cause any sin, opposing cities if they add any sin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical evaluation of asceticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Asceticism is judged by whether its suppression of desires and avoidance of temptation contributes positively to moral progress or leads to 'tame, languid, and mutilated natures' lacking energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ascetics consistently avoid external temptations and pursue sinlessness, which is coherent given their premises; but excessively prioritising diminution of sin can weaken moral character and reduce other valuable human capacities. Historical decline of ascetic practices is cited as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness and indeterminacy of moral boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral qualities often lack sharp boundaries; colours of moral nature 'fade and blend' so that precise transition points between lawful and illicit cannot generally be drawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intuitive moralist accepts only general principles and leaves application to individual conscience or societal sentiment; disputes over entertainments, amusements, or customs illustrate gradations rather than discrete rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of utilitarian certainty: impossibility of measuring different utilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The utilitarian claim to possess a definite formulary for drawing clear lines between lawful and illicit actions is problematic because there is no common measure enabling accurate comparison of different kinds of utility or happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: weighing intellectual/physical advantages of an excursion train against moral evils (drunkenness, increased vice). The text argues it's impossible to reduce such judgments to precise arithmetic of happiness; utilitarians cannot reliably balance incommensurable goods and evils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive-based moral valuation: selfishness detracts from virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: An action motivated by selfish considerations (fear of punishment, personal gain) is not regarded as morally meritorious even if its outward conduct conforms to duty; mixed motives reduce moral credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a thief refrains only because of a policeman's presence—this abstinence lacks moral value. However, institutions of reward and punishment may reinforce virtuous motives and help habituate moral behaviour over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic value of some virtues vs occasional overriding by extreme utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Some virtues possess intrinsic excellence not proportional to their utility; nevertheless, in rare cases of overwhelming utility, these virtues may be sacrificed (e.g., lying to save an innocent life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognises two claims: (1) pursuit of others' welfare is a genuine form of virtue but not the whole of virtue; (2) extreme public utility can sometimes justify overriding non-utilitarian virtues. Illustrative cases include enterprises producing material good but some crime, or tacitly tolerating false beliefs for public benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning against equivocation in 'natural' (the 'natural man' problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'natural man' is ambiguous—sometimes meaning primitive/barbarous, sometimes meaning what is due to nature rather than acquired habits; conflating these leads to fallacious arguments about absence of moral sense in savages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports of savages lacking moral sentiments are often unreliable; even if accurate, dormant moral faculties may be present and require favorable conditions (education, social environment) for development. Analogy: acorn vs stone—capacity for development distinguishes humans from brutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of moral conceptions: sensation (empiricism) vs intuition (a priori faculties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two foundational criteria for evaluating moral theories: whether moral ideas derive entirely from sensation and experience, or partly from innate mental faculties or intuitions that are independent of sensory experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically linked to schools: Locke/Condillac/empiricists (morals of interest/utilitarian tendencies) versus Platonic/Leibniz/Kantian and Scottish/German idealists (asserting moral faculty/intuition). The choice influences the form and emphasis of ethical systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical / civilisational criterion: relative weight of invention/science versus moral qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging the progress or superiority of societies, consider whether priority is given to moral/intellectual qualities or to physical science, inventive skill, and industrial enterprise; modern prominence of inventions changes how superiority is assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: printing preserves intellectual achievements; gunpowder/steam changed military and industrial balance. The text suggests practical/inventive success often explains modern national superiority more than sustained moral energy, affecting how one assesses a society's moral status.
